TrueCrypt is safer than previously reported, detailed analysis concludes

...there's no indication that they can be exploited to provide attackers access to encrypted data stored on an unmounted hard drive or thumb drive.

Um... well, to be perfectly honest, an unencrypted drive that is disconnected is also pretty secure from attackers. I would challenge any remote users to attack my system here at work and use that attack vector to access the thumb drive I have sitting on my desk at home.

"Unmounted" in this sense doesn't mean physically disconnected. When you use TruCrypt to encrypt data, you create a virtual encrypted drive that can be "mounted" by the TruCrypt software. The encrypted data will then show up within TruCrypt as a standard drive letter with its data unencrypted and clear. This is an important distinction to make because while your data is mounted it's 100% decrypted and in the clear. It's only while the data is "at rest" and unmounted that it's secured again.

In the sentence that you're quoting, the researchers are saying that while TruCrypt has been the focus of a recent security breach, that security breach only allows a malicious program to exploit a part of TruCrypt's software to grant itself more privileges in the OS. While this is certainly a problem it doesn't mean that the security exploit will allow access to your "unmounted" and encrypted data, which is the point the researchers wanted to stress.
